target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove the main barrier to voting by giving people time off
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably solve the time-off problem because private employers are not required by federal law to close or give paid leave, so many workers—especially in retail, food service, hospitals, and other service jobs—would still be scheduled to work and might still be unable to vote.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would broadly help all voters
objection: A national holiday could disadvantage low-income workers because salaried or unionized employees may benefit from existing holiday policies while hourly workers can still be required to work or lose pay, so the policy may help people with more flexible jobs more than those with the least flexibility.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that a holiday is the best way to improve access
objection: State-level reforms that directly require employers to provide voting time off, along with other measures like automatic voter registration, early voting, and vote-by-mail, are more dependable and effective than simply making Election Day a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would meaningfully increase turnout on its own
objection: Research suggests that declaring Election Day a holiday by itself is not as effective at increasing turnout as targeted voting-access reforms such as guaranteed time to vote, expanded early voting, vote-by-mail, and automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday will not reliably solve the time-off problem because private employers can still schedule workers
objection: A national holiday changes the default scheduling environment: schools, public services, and many private-sector operations typically reduce activity on holidays, which lowers the number of people facing inflexible work shifts on election day and makes voting easier even without a universal paid-leave mandate.

target: AG2’s claim that workers still face the same barrier if some employers stay open
objection: Even if some employers remain open, a holiday still helps because it creates a time when people are more likely to have uninterrupted availability, better transportation, and fewer childcare or school-related conflicts, so it meaningfully reduces logistical barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that other reforms are preferable to a holiday
objection: A holiday is complementary rather than competing with other reforms: it lowers baseline friction for everyone and elevates voting into a shared civic event, which can increase planning and participation.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would change the scheduling environment enough to help workers generally
objection: The key problem is concentrated in hourly, low-wage, customer-facing jobs in retail, service, and healthcare support, where workplaces often do not close even on holidays; for those workers, the holiday does not remove the barrier and can leave them with lost wages if they take time off.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday creates a meaningful baseline for access
objection: A holiday label is mostly symbolic unless it is paired with a legal time-off requirement or direct voting-time protections; a policy that actually mandates paid or job-protected time to vote is more consistent and more likely to benefit low-income workers.

target: AG2’s objection that a holiday does not force private employers to close or provide paid leave
objection: The purpose of a national holiday is not to eliminate every work conflict but to shift default conditions and employer incentives; many institutions already reduce staffing or offer time off on holidays, so the policy still helps many hourly and customer-facing workers.

target: AG2’s assumption that election-day barriers are only about getting formal time off
objection: Voting barriers also include childcare and weekday logistics, because school schedules and regular routines shape people’s ability to get to the polls; a holiday makes those supports more available and reduces the practical burden on families and shift workers.

target: AG2’s reliance on state-by-state reforms as the preferred approach
objection: A national holiday provides a consistent baseline across the country, so access does not depend on where someone lives or works, whereas state-by-state approaches leave protections uneven.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday meaningfully improves logistics like childcare availability
objection: That logic can backfire because low-cost childcare options tied to school schedules may close or reduce hours on holidays, and essential retail/service workers may still have to work, making the holiday burdensome for low-income families rather than helpful.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday provides a useful baseline across jurisdictions
objection: A calendar change is mostly symbolic unless it comes with legally guaranteed paid or job-protected time to vote; the more consistent policy is to mandate time off or expand access directly through early voting, vote-by-mail, and automatic registration.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday effects are limited because they do not force all employers to close or pay leave
objection: A national holiday still changes incentives and schedules enough to reduce barriers for many voters, and because it is intended as a complement to other access reforms, it should not be dismissed just because it is not sufficient on its own.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday-related logistics do not reliably help low-income voters
objection: The holiday can still improve the broader civic environment by increasing predictability and making voting feel like a normal, shared part of civic life rather than an inconvenient chore, which supports participation beyond just formal time-off rules.

target: AG2’s criticism that a holiday may not affect childcare or schedules enough
objection: Because many institutions reduce operations on national holidays, the policy can make transportation, childcare, and weekday routine conflicts less severe for many households, even if it does not solve every case.

target: AG1’s framing of holiday benefits as useful because they can complement other reforms
objection: If other measures like paid/job-protected time off, early voting, vote-by-mail, and automatic registration are still necessary, then making Election Day a holiday is largely redundant and potentially misleading as a centerpiece policy.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday helps low-income workers even without employer mandates
objection: Because private employers are not required to close or provide holiday pay, many hourly workers would still face the same wage tradeoff and could lose hours or take unpaid leave, while people whose employers already grant holidays would benefit more—so the policy does not reliably target the biggest turnout bottleneck for low-income voters.

target: AG1’s broader claim that a holiday is a practical turnout measure
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy; the better approach is state rules guaranteeing time to vote and other access reforms that directly change workers’ ability to participate.
